The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 2, 2024. The two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election on November 5, 2024. A primary was scheduled for March 19, 2024. The filing deadline was December 4, 2023.

With a total of seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court"), two justices, one from each party, ran for re-election without opposition. As of April 2024, five judges on the court were Democrats and two judges were Republicans and no overall partisan change is expected in the November 5, 2024 election.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024#cite_note-1)

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Judicial selection in Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial\_selection\_in\_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois")_
Each of the seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") serves terms of 10 years. In the case of a vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. If a justice is appointed more than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") in the next general or judicial election to remain on the court. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election. If a justice is appointed less than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice will have to run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to remain on the court in the second general election. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024#cite_note-ILselect-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a judge must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024#cite_note-ILselect-2)

The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 2, 2024. The two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election on November 5, 2024. A primary was scheduled for March 19, 2024. The filing deadline was December 4, 2023.

With a total of seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court"), two justices, one from each party, ran for re-election without opposition. As of April 2024, five judges on the court were Democrats and two judges were Republicans and no overall partisan change is expected in the November 5, 2024 election.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024#cite_note-1)

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Judicial selection in Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial\_selection\_in\_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois")_
Each of the seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") serves terms of 10 years. In the case of a vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. If a justice is appointed more than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") in the next general or judicial election to remain on the court. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election. If a justice is appointed less than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice will have to run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to remain on the court in the second general election. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024#cite_note-ILselect-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a judge must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024#cite_note-ILselect-2)

[Elizabeth M. Rochford](https://ballotpedia.org/Elizabeth_M._Rochford "Elizabeth M. Rochford") (D) defeated [Mark Curran](https://ballotpedia.org/Mark_Curran "Mark Curran") (R), and [Mary O'Brien](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_O%27Brien "Mary O'Brien") (D) defeated [Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke") (R) in partisan elections for two Illinois Supreme Court seats on November 8, 2022. Chief Justice [Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis") (D) won a retention vote for her seat.

As a result of these elections, the court composition will change from a 4-3 Democratic majority to a 5-2 Democratic majority in 2023.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-Tribune-1)

The terms of the three [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired in 2022. One judicial term expired on December 4, 2022, and two judicial terms expired on December 5, 2022.

A retention election for [Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman") was canceled after Garman retired effective July 7, 2022. [Lisa Holder White](https://ballotpedia.org/Lisa_Holder_White "Lisa Holder White") was [appointed to the seat](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial_selection_in_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois"), which was up for partisan election in 2024.

The _Chicago Tribune's_ John Keilman said, "Democrats held a 4-3 advantage on the court prior to Election Day, and the party cast the contested races as a referendum on abortion. Commercials by the candidates and their backers contended that electing Republicans would endanger that right in Illinois."[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-Tribune-1)

"The Republicans, meanwhile, aimed to portray their opponents as products of the state’s Democratic machine who owed their careers to indicted former House Speaker Michael Madigan and other power brokers," Keilman said.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-Tribune-1)  
  
Illinois was one of 30 states that held elections for state supreme court in 2022. That year, 84 of the 344 seats on state supreme courts were up for election. Of those, 64 were held by nonpartisan justices, 13 were held by Republican justices, and eight were held by Democratic justices. For more on the partisan affiliation of state supreme court justices, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_State_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship"). For an overview of state supreme court elections in 2022, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/State_supreme_court_elections,_2022 "State supreme court elections, 2022").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

## Analysis

### Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters (2021)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_
![Image 34: Ballotpedia Courts Determiners and Dissenters navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/bb/Ballotpedia_Courts_Determiners_and_Dissenters_navigation_ad.png) In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_, a study on how state supreme court justices decided the cases that came before them. Our goal was to determine which justices ruled together most often, which frequently dissented, and which courts featured the most unanimous or contentious decisions.

The study tracked the position taken by each state supreme court justice in every case they decided in 2020, then tallied the number of times the justices on the court ruled together. We identified the following types of justices:

*   We considered two justices _**opinion partners**_ if they frequently concurred or dissented together throughout the year.
*   We considered justices a _**dissenting minority**_ if they frequently opposed decisions together as a -1 minority.
*   We considered a group of justices a _**determining majority**_ if they frequently determined cases by a +1 majority throughout the year.
*   We considered a justice a _**lone dissenter**_ if he or she frequently dissented alone in cases throughout the year.

#### Summary of cases decided in 2020

*   Number of justices: 7
*   Number of cases: 63
*   Percentage of cases with a unanimous ruling: 69.8%% (44)
*   Justice most often writing the majority opinion: Justice Theis (11)
*   Per curiam decisions: 2
*   Concurring opinions: 7
*   Justice with most concurring opinions: Justices A. Burke, Karmeier, and Kilbride (2)
*   Dissenting opinions: 20
*   Justice with most dissenting opinions: Justice Neville (8)

For the study's full set of findings in Illinois, click [here](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_Determiners_and_Dissenters/Illinois "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters/Illinois").

### Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship (2020)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_
![Image 35: Ballotpedia Courts State Partisanship navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/b6/Ballotpedia_Courts_State_Partisanship_navigation_ad.png)_Last updated: June 15, 2020_

In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_, a study examining the partisan affiliation of all state supreme court justices in the country as of June 15, 2020.

The study presented _Confidence Scores_ that represented our confidence in each justice's degree of partisan affiliation, based on a variety of factors. This was not a measure of where a justice fell on the political or ideological spectrum, but rather a measure of how much confidence we had that a justice was or had been affiliated with a political party. To arrive at confidence scores we analyzed each justice's past partisan activity by collecting data on campaign finance, past political positions, party registration history, as well as other factors. The five categories of _Confidence Scores_ were:

*   Strong Democrat
*   Mild Democrat
*   Indeterminate[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-3)
*   Mild Republican
*   Strong Republican

We used the Confidence Scores of each justice to develop a Court Balance Score, which attempted to show the balance among justices with Democratic, Republican, and Indeterminate Confidence Scores on a court. Courts with higher positive Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Republican Confidence Scores, while courts with lower negative Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Democratic Confidence Scores. Courts closest to zero either had justices with conflicting partisanship or justices with Indeterminate Confidence Scores.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-4)

Illinois had a Court Balance Score of **-4**, indicating **Democratic control** of the court. In total, the study found that there were 15 states with Democrat-controlled courts, 27 states with Republican-controlled courts, and eight states with Split courts. [Elizabeth M. Rochford](https://ballotpedia.org/Elizabeth_M._Rochford "Elizabeth M. Rochford") (D) defeated [Mark Curran](https://ballotpedia.org/Mark_Curran "Mark Curran") (R), and [Mary O'Brien](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_O%27Brien "Mary O'Brien") (D) defeated [Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke") (R) in partisan elections for two Illinois Supreme Court seats on November 8, 2022. Chief Justice [Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis") (D) won a retention vote for her seat.

As a result of these elections, the court composition will change from a 4-3 Democratic majority to a 5-2 Democratic majority in 2023.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-Tribune-1)

The terms of the three [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired in 2022. One judicial term expired on December 4, 2022, and two judicial terms expired on December 5, 2022.

A retention election for [Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman") was canceled after Garman retired effective July 7, 2022. [Lisa Holder White](https://ballotpedia.org/Lisa_Holder_White "Lisa Holder White") was [appointed to the seat](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial_selection_in_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois"), which was up for partisan election in 2024.

The _Chicago Tribune's_ John Keilman said, "Democrats held a 4-3 advantage on the court prior to Election Day, and the party cast the contested races as a referendum on abortion. Commercials by the candidates and their backers contended that electing Republicans would endanger that right in Illinois."[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-Tribune-1)

"The Republicans, meanwhile, aimed to portray their opponents as products of the state’s Democratic machine who owed their careers to indicted former House Speaker Michael Madigan and other power brokers," Keilman said.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-Tribune-1)  
  
Illinois was one of 30 states that held elections for state supreme court in 2022. That year, 84 of the 344 seats on state supreme courts were up for election. Of those, 64 were held by nonpartisan justices, 13 were held by Republican justices, and eight were held by Democratic justices. For more on the partisan affiliation of state supreme court justices, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_State_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship"). For an overview of state supreme court elections in 2022, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/State_supreme_court_elections,_2022 "State supreme court elections, 2022").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-gen-2)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

## Analysis

### Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters (2021)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_
![Image 34: Ballotpedia Courts Determiners and Dissenters navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/bb/Ballotpedia_Courts_Determiners_and_Dissenters_navigation_ad.png) In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_, a study on how state supreme court justices decided the cases that came before them. Our goal was to determine which justices ruled together most often, which frequently dissented, and which courts featured the most unanimous or contentious decisions.

The study tracked the position taken by each state supreme court justice in every case they decided in 2020, then tallied the number of times the justices on the court ruled together. We identified the following types of justices:

*   We considered two justices _**opinion partners**_ if they frequently concurred or dissented together throughout the year.
*   We considered justices a _**dissenting minority**_ if they frequently opposed decisions together as a -1 minority.
*   We considered a group of justices a _**determining majority**_ if they frequently determined cases by a +1 majority throughout the year.
*   We considered a justice a _**lone dissenter**_ if he or she frequently dissented alone in cases throughout the year.

#### Summary of cases decided in 2020

*   Number of justices: 7
*   Number of cases: 63
*   Percentage of cases with a unanimous ruling: 69.8%% (44)
*   Justice most often writing the majority opinion: Justice Theis (11)
*   Per curiam decisions: 2
*   Concurring opinions: 7
*   Justice with most concurring opinions: Justices A. Burke, Karmeier, and Kilbride (2)
*   Dissenting opinions: 20
*   Justice with most dissenting opinions: Justice Neville (8)

For the study's full set of findings in Illinois, click [here](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_Determiners_and_Dissenters/Illinois "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters/Illinois").

### Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship (2020)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_
![Image 35: Ballotpedia Courts State Partisanship navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/b6/Ballotpedia_Courts_State_Partisanship_navigation_ad.png)_Last updated: June 15, 2020_

In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_, a study examining the partisan affiliation of all state supreme court justices in the country as of June 15, 2020.

The study presented _Confidence Scores_ that represented our confidence in each justice's degree of partisan affiliation, based on a variety of factors. This was not a measure of where a justice fell on the political or ideological spectrum, but rather a measure of how much confidence we had that a justice was or had been affiliated with a political party. To arrive at confidence scores we analyzed each justice's past partisan activity by collecting data on campaign finance, past political positions, party registration history, as well as other factors. The five categories of _Confidence Scores_ were:

*   Strong Democrat
*   Mild Democrat
*   Indeterminate[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-3)
*   Mild Republican
*   Strong Republican

We used the Confidence Scores of each justice to develop a Court Balance Score, which attempted to show the balance among justices with Democratic, Republican, and Indeterminate Confidence Scores on a court. Courts with higher positive Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Republican Confidence Scores, while courts with lower negative Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Democratic Confidence Scores. Courts closest to zero either had justices with conflicting partisanship or justices with Indeterminate Confidence Scores.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022#cite_note-4)

Illinois had a Court Balance Score of **-4**, indicating **Democratic control** of the court. In total, the study found that there were 15 states with Democrat-controlled courts, 27 states with Republican-controlled courts, and eight states with Split courts. 4.   ↑The Court Balance Score is calculated by finding the average partisan Confidence Score of all justices on a state supreme court. For example, if a state has justices on the state supreme court with Confidence Scores of 4, -2, 2, 14, -2, 3, and 4, the Court Balance is the average of those scores: 3.3. Therefore, the Confidence Score on the court is Mild Republican. The use of positive and negative numbers in presenting both Confidence Scores and Court Balance Scores should not be understood to that either a Republican or Democratic score is _positive_ or _negative._ The numerical values represent their distance from zero, not whether one score is better or worse than another.

The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 7, 2020. A special election also took place to replace Justice [Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier") (R) who retired December 6, 2020. Two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election and one seat was up for retention election on November 3, 2020. A primary was scheduled for March 17, 2020.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-1)

The filing deadline for partisan elections was December 2, 2019. The filing deadline for retention elections was May 3, 2020.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-2)

Ballotpedia provided comprehensive coverage of how election dates and procedures changed in 2020. While the majority of changes occurred as a result of the [coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic](https://ballotpedia.org/Documenting_America%27s_Path_to_Recovery "Documenting America's Path to Recovery"), some changes occurred for other reasons.

Illinois modified its absentee/mail-in voting and candidate filing procedures for the November 3, 2020, general election as follows:

*   **Absentee/mail-in voting**: Mail-in ballot applications were sent to all registered voters in the general election who cast ballots in the 2018 general election, the 2019 consolidated election, or the 2020 primary election.
*   **Candidate filing procedures**: The following changes were made to the filing procedures for unaffiliated and new-party candidates: petition signature requirements were reduced to 10 percent of their original numbers; candidates were authorized to collect petition signatures electronically; and the filing deadline was extended to July 20, 2020.

For a full timeline about election modifications made in response to the COVID-19 outbreak, [click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes_to_election_dates,_procedures,_and_administration_in_response_to_the_coronavirus_(COVID-19)_pandemic,_2020#Illinois "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 7, 2020. A special election also took place to replace Justice [Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier") (R) who retired December 6, 2020. Two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election and one seat was up for retention election on November 3, 2020. A primary was scheduled for March 17, 2020.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-1)

The filing deadline for partisan elections was December 2, 2019. The filing deadline for retention elections was May 3, 2020.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-2)

## Election procedure changes in 2020

_See also: [Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes\_to\_election\_dates,\_procedures,\_and\_administration\_in\_response\_to\_the\_coronavirus\_(COVID-19)\_pandemic,\_2020 "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020")_
Ballotpedia provided comprehensive coverage of how election dates and procedures changed in 2020. While the majority of changes occurred as a result of the [coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic](https://ballotpedia.org/Documenting_America%27s_Path_to_Recovery "Documenting America's Path to Recovery"), some changes occurred for other reasons.

Illinois modified its absentee/mail-in voting and candidate filing procedures for the November 3, 2020, general election as follows:

*   **Absentee/mail-in voting**: Mail-in ballot applications were sent to all registered voters in the general election who cast ballots in the 2018 general election, the 2019 consolidated election, or the 2020 primary election.
*   **Candidate filing procedures**: The following changes were made to the filing procedures for unaffiliated and new-party candidates: petition signature requirements were reduced to 10 percent of their original numbers; candidates were authorized to collect petition signatures electronically; and the filing deadline was extended to July 20, 2020.

For a full timeline about election modifications made in response to the COVID-19 outbreak, [click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes_to_election_dates,_procedures,_and_administration_in_response_to_the_coronavirus_(COVID-19)_pandemic,_2020#Illinois "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

### Political composition

This was the political composition of the supreme court heading into the 2020 election.

■[Anne M. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Anne_M._Burke "Anne M. Burke")_Appointed in 2006; elected in 2008_
■[Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman")_Appointed in 2001; elected in 2002; retained in 2012_
■[Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier")_Elected in 2004; retained in 2014_
■[Thomas Kilbride](https://ballotpedia.org/Thomas_Kilbride "Thomas Kilbride")_Elected in 2000; retained in 2010_
■[P. Scott Neville](https://ballotpedia.org/P._Scott_Neville "P. Scott Neville")_Appointed in 2018_
■[Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis")_Appointed in 2010; elected in 2012_
■[Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke")_Appointed in 2020_

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020#cite_note-gen-6)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 2, 2024. The two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election on November 5, 2024. A primary was scheduled for March 19, 2024. The filing deadline was December 4, 2023.

With a total of seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court"), two justices, one from each party, ran for re-election without opposition. As of April 2024, five judges on the court were Democrats and two judges were Republicans and no overall partisan change is expected in the November 5, 2024 election.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024?printable=yes#cite_note-1)

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Judicial selection in Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial\_selection\_in\_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois")_
Each of the seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") serves terms of 10 years. In the case of a vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. If a justice is appointed more than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") in the next general or judicial election to remain on the court. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election. If a justice is appointed less than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice will have to run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to remain on the court in the second general election. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024?printable=yes#cite_note-ILselect-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a judge must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024?printable=yes#cite_note-ILselect-2)

The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 2, 2024. The two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election on November 5, 2024. A primary was scheduled for March 19, 2024. The filing deadline was December 4, 2023.

With a total of seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court"), two justices, one from each party, ran for re-election without opposition. As of April 2024, five judges on the court were Democrats and two judges were Republicans and no overall partisan change is expected in the November 5, 2024 election.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024?printable=yes#cite_note-1)

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Judicial selection in Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial\_selection\_in\_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois")_
Each of the seven justices on the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") serves terms of 10 years. In the case of a vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. If a justice is appointed more than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") in the next general or judicial election to remain on the court. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election. If a justice is appointed less than 60 days before the next primary election, the justice will have to run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to remain on the court in the second general election. The appointed justice's term will end on the first Monday in December after their election[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024?printable=yes#cite_note-ILselect-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a judge must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2024?printable=yes#cite_note-ILselect-2)

[Elizabeth M. Rochford](https://ballotpedia.org/Elizabeth_M._Rochford "Elizabeth M. Rochford") (D) defeated [Mark Curran](https://ballotpedia.org/Mark_Curran "Mark Curran") (R), and [Mary O'Brien](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_O%27Brien "Mary O'Brien") (D) defeated [Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke") (R) in partisan elections for two Illinois Supreme Court seats on November 8, 2022. Chief Justice [Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis") (D) won a retention vote for her seat.

As a result of these elections, the court composition will change from a 4-3 Democratic majority to a 5-2 Democratic majority in 2023.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-Tribune-1)

The terms of the three [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired in 2022. One judicial term expired on December 4, 2022, and two judicial terms expired on December 5, 2022.

A retention election for [Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman") was canceled after Garman retired effective July 7, 2022. [Lisa Holder White](https://ballotpedia.org/Lisa_Holder_White "Lisa Holder White") was [appointed to the seat](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial_selection_in_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois"), which was up for partisan election in 2024.

The _Chicago Tribune's_ John Keilman said, "Democrats held a 4-3 advantage on the court prior to Election Day, and the party cast the contested races as a referendum on abortion. Commercials by the candidates and their backers contended that electing Republicans would endanger that right in Illinois."[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-Tribune-1)

"The Republicans, meanwhile, aimed to portray their opponents as products of the state’s Democratic machine who owed their careers to indicted former House Speaker Michael Madigan and other power brokers," Keilman said.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-Tribune-1)  
  
Illinois was one of 30 states that held elections for state supreme court in 2022. That year, 84 of the 344 seats on state supreme courts were up for election. Of those, 64 were held by nonpartisan justices, 13 were held by Republican justices, and eight were held by Democratic justices. For more on the partisan affiliation of state supreme court justices, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_State_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship"). For an overview of state supreme court elections in 2022, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/State_supreme_court_elections,_2022 "State supreme court elections, 2022").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

## Analysis

### Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters (2021)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_
![Image 34: Ballotpedia Courts Determiners and Dissenters navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/bb/Ballotpedia_Courts_Determiners_and_Dissenters_navigation_ad.png) In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_, a study on how state supreme court justices decided the cases that came before them. Our goal was to determine which justices ruled together most often, which frequently dissented, and which courts featured the most unanimous or contentious decisions.

The study tracked the position taken by each state supreme court justice in every case they decided in 2020, then tallied the number of times the justices on the court ruled together. We identified the following types of justices:

*   We considered two justices _**opinion partners**_ if they frequently concurred or dissented together throughout the year.
*   We considered justices a _**dissenting minority**_ if they frequently opposed decisions together as a -1 minority.
*   We considered a group of justices a _**determining majority**_ if they frequently determined cases by a +1 majority throughout the year.
*   We considered a justice a _**lone dissenter**_ if he or she frequently dissented alone in cases throughout the year.

#### Summary of cases decided in 2020

*   Number of justices: 7
*   Number of cases: 63
*   Percentage of cases with a unanimous ruling: 69.8%% (44)
*   Justice most often writing the majority opinion: Justice Theis (11)
*   Per curiam decisions: 2
*   Concurring opinions: 7
*   Justice with most concurring opinions: Justices A. Burke, Karmeier, and Kilbride (2)
*   Dissenting opinions: 20
*   Justice with most dissenting opinions: Justice Neville (8)

For the study's full set of findings in Illinois, click [here](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_Determiners_and_Dissenters/Illinois "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters/Illinois").

### Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship (2020)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_
![Image 35: Ballotpedia Courts State Partisanship navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/b6/Ballotpedia_Courts_State_Partisanship_navigation_ad.png)_Last updated: June 15, 2020_

In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_, a study examining the partisan affiliation of all state supreme court justices in the country as of June 15, 2020.

The study presented _Confidence Scores_ that represented our confidence in each justice's degree of partisan affiliation, based on a variety of factors. This was not a measure of where a justice fell on the political or ideological spectrum, but rather a measure of how much confidence we had that a justice was or had been affiliated with a political party. To arrive at confidence scores we analyzed each justice's past partisan activity by collecting data on campaign finance, past political positions, party registration history, as well as other factors. The five categories of _Confidence Scores_ were:

*   Strong Democrat
*   Mild Democrat
*   Indeterminate[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-3)
*   Mild Republican
*   Strong Republican

We used the Confidence Scores of each justice to develop a Court Balance Score, which attempted to show the balance among justices with Democratic, Republican, and Indeterminate Confidence Scores on a court. Courts with higher positive Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Republican Confidence Scores, while courts with lower negative Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Democratic Confidence Scores. Courts closest to zero either had justices with conflicting partisanship or justices with Indeterminate Confidence Scores.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-4)

Illinois had a Court Balance Score of **-4**, indicating **Democratic control** of the court. In total, the study found that there were 15 states with Democrat-controlled courts, 27 states with Republican-controlled courts, and eight states with Split courts. [Elizabeth M. Rochford](https://ballotpedia.org/Elizabeth_M._Rochford "Elizabeth M. Rochford") (D) defeated [Mark Curran](https://ballotpedia.org/Mark_Curran "Mark Curran") (R), and [Mary O'Brien](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_O%27Brien "Mary O'Brien") (D) defeated [Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke") (R) in partisan elections for two Illinois Supreme Court seats on November 8, 2022. Chief Justice [Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis") (D) won a retention vote for her seat.

As a result of these elections, the court composition will change from a 4-3 Democratic majority to a 5-2 Democratic majority in 2023.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-Tribune-1)

The terms of the three [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired in 2022. One judicial term expired on December 4, 2022, and two judicial terms expired on December 5, 2022.

A retention election for [Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman") was canceled after Garman retired effective July 7, 2022. [Lisa Holder White](https://ballotpedia.org/Lisa_Holder_White "Lisa Holder White") was [appointed to the seat](https://ballotpedia.org/Judicial_selection_in_Illinois "Judicial selection in Illinois"), which was up for partisan election in 2024.

The _Chicago Tribune's_ John Keilman said, "Democrats held a 4-3 advantage on the court prior to Election Day, and the party cast the contested races as a referendum on abortion. Commercials by the candidates and their backers contended that electing Republicans would endanger that right in Illinois."[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-Tribune-1)

"The Republicans, meanwhile, aimed to portray their opponents as products of the state’s Democratic machine who owed their careers to indicted former House Speaker Michael Madigan and other power brokers," Keilman said.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-Tribune-1)  
  
Illinois was one of 30 states that held elections for state supreme court in 2022. That year, 84 of the 344 seats on state supreme courts were up for election. Of those, 64 were held by nonpartisan justices, 13 were held by Republican justices, and eight were held by Democratic justices. For more on the partisan affiliation of state supreme court justices, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_State_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship"). For an overview of state supreme court elections in 2022, click [**here**](https://ballotpedia.org/State_supreme_court_elections,_2022 "State supreme court elections, 2022").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-2)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

## Analysis

### Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters (2021)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_
![Image 34: Ballotpedia Courts Determiners and Dissenters navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/bb/Ballotpedia_Courts_Determiners_and_Dissenters_navigation_ad.png) In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_Determiners\_and\_Dissenters "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters")_, a study on how state supreme court justices decided the cases that came before them. Our goal was to determine which justices ruled together most often, which frequently dissented, and which courts featured the most unanimous or contentious decisions.

The study tracked the position taken by each state supreme court justice in every case they decided in 2020, then tallied the number of times the justices on the court ruled together. We identified the following types of justices:

*   We considered two justices _**opinion partners**_ if they frequently concurred or dissented together throughout the year.
*   We considered justices a _**dissenting minority**_ if they frequently opposed decisions together as a -1 minority.
*   We considered a group of justices a _**determining majority**_ if they frequently determined cases by a +1 majority throughout the year.
*   We considered a justice a _**lone dissenter**_ if he or she frequently dissented alone in cases throughout the year.

#### Summary of cases decided in 2020

*   Number of justices: 7
*   Number of cases: 63
*   Percentage of cases with a unanimous ruling: 69.8%% (44)
*   Justice most often writing the majority opinion: Justice Theis (11)
*   Per curiam decisions: 2
*   Concurring opinions: 7
*   Justice with most concurring opinions: Justices A. Burke, Karmeier, and Kilbride (2)
*   Dissenting opinions: 20
*   Justice with most dissenting opinions: Justice Neville (8)

For the study's full set of findings in Illinois, click [here](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Courts:_Determiners_and_Dissenters/Illinois "Ballotpedia Courts: Determiners and Dissenters/Illinois").

### Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship (2020)

_See also: [Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_
![Image 35: Ballotpedia Courts State Partisanship navigation ad.png](https://ballotpedia.s3.amazonaws.com/images/b/b6/Ballotpedia_Courts_State_Partisanship_navigation_ad.png)_Last updated: June 15, 2020_

In 2020, Ballotpedia published _[Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia\_Courts:\_State\_Partisanship "Ballotpedia Courts: State Partisanship")_, a study examining the partisan affiliation of all state supreme court justices in the country as of June 15, 2020.

The study presented _Confidence Scores_ that represented our confidence in each justice's degree of partisan affiliation, based on a variety of factors. This was not a measure of where a justice fell on the political or ideological spectrum, but rather a measure of how much confidence we had that a justice was or had been affiliated with a political party. To arrive at confidence scores we analyzed each justice's past partisan activity by collecting data on campaign finance, past political positions, party registration history, as well as other factors. The five categories of _Confidence Scores_ were:

*   Strong Democrat
*   Mild Democrat
*   Indeterminate[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-3)
*   Mild Republican
*   Strong Republican

We used the Confidence Scores of each justice to develop a Court Balance Score, which attempted to show the balance among justices with Democratic, Republican, and Indeterminate Confidence Scores on a court. Courts with higher positive Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Republican Confidence Scores, while courts with lower negative Court Balance Scores included justices with higher Democratic Confidence Scores. Courts closest to zero either had justices with conflicting partisanship or justices with Indeterminate Confidence Scores.[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2022?printable=yes#cite_note-4)

Illinois had a Court Balance Score of **-4**, indicating **Democratic control** of the court. In total, the study found that there were 15 states with Democrat-controlled courts, 27 states with Republican-controlled courts, and eight states with Split courts. The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 7, 2020. A special election also took place to replace Justice [Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier") (R) who retired December 6, 2020. Two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election and one seat was up for retention election on November 3, 2020. A primary was scheduled for March 17, 2020.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-1)

The filing deadline for partisan elections was December 2, 2019. The filing deadline for retention elections was May 3, 2020.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-2)

## Election procedure changes in 2020

_See also: [Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes\_to\_election\_dates,\_procedures,\_and\_administration\_in\_response\_to\_the\_coronavirus\_(COVID-19)\_pandemic,\_2020 "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020")_
Ballotpedia provided comprehensive coverage of how election dates and procedures changed in 2020. While the majority of changes occurred as a result of the [coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic](https://ballotpedia.org/Documenting_America%27s_Path_to_Recovery "Documenting America's Path to Recovery"), some changes occurred for other reasons.

Illinois modified its absentee/mail-in voting and candidate filing procedures for the November 3, 2020, general election as follows:

*   **Absentee/mail-in voting**: Mail-in ballot applications were sent to all registered voters in the general election who cast ballots in the 2018 general election, the 2019 consolidated election, or the 2020 primary election.
*   **Candidate filing procedures**: The following changes were made to the filing procedures for unaffiliated and new-party candidates: petition signature requirements were reduced to 10 percent of their original numbers; candidates were authorized to collect petition signatures electronically; and the filing deadline was extended to July 20, 2020.

For a full timeline about election modifications made in response to the COVID-19 outbreak, [click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes_to_election_dates,_procedures,_and_administration_in_response_to_the_coronavirus_(COVID-19)_pandemic,_2020#Illinois "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

### Political composition

This was the political composition of the supreme court heading into the 2020 election.

■[Anne M. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Anne_M._Burke "Anne M. Burke")_Appointed in 2006; elected in 2008_
■[Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman")_Appointed in 2001; elected in 2002; retained in 2012_
■[Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier")_Elected in 2004; retained in 2014_
■[Thomas Kilbride](https://ballotpedia.org/Thomas_Kilbride "Thomas Kilbride")_Elected in 2000; retained in 2010_
■[P. Scott Neville](https://ballotpedia.org/P._Scott_Neville "P. Scott Neville")_Appointed in 2018_
■[Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis")_Appointed in 2010; elected in 2012_
■[Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke")_Appointed in 2020_

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.

The terms of two [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") justices expired on December 7, 2020. A special election also took place to replace Justice [Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier") (R) who retired December 6, 2020. Two seats were up for [partisan](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges") election and one seat was up for retention election on November 3, 2020. A primary was scheduled for March 17, 2020.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-1)

The filing deadline for partisan elections was December 2, 2019. The filing deadline for retention elections was May 3, 2020.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-2)

## Election procedure changes in 2020

_See also: [Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes\_to\_election\_dates,\_procedures,\_and\_administration\_in\_response\_to\_the\_coronavirus\_(COVID-19)\_pandemic,\_2020 "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020")_
Ballotpedia provided comprehensive coverage of how election dates and procedures changed in 2020. While the majority of changes occurred as a result of the [coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic](https://ballotpedia.org/Documenting_America%27s_Path_to_Recovery "Documenting America's Path to Recovery"), some changes occurred for other reasons.

Illinois modified its absentee/mail-in voting and candidate filing procedures for the November 3, 2020, general election as follows:

*   **Absentee/mail-in voting**: Mail-in ballot applications were sent to all registered voters in the general election who cast ballots in the 2018 general election, the 2019 consolidated election, or the 2020 primary election.
*   **Candidate filing procedures**: The following changes were made to the filing procedures for unaffiliated and new-party candidates: petition signature requirements were reduced to 10 percent of their original numbers; candidates were authorized to collect petition signatures electronically; and the filing deadline was extended to July 20, 2020.

For a full timeline about election modifications made in response to the COVID-19 outbreak, [click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Changes_to_election_dates,_procedures,_and_administration_in_response_to_the_coronavirus_(COVID-19)_pandemic,_2020#Illinois "Changes to election dates, procedures, and administration in response to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, 2020").

## About the Illinois Supreme Court

_See also: [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois\_Supreme\_Court "Illinois Supreme Court")_
The Illinois Supreme Court is the [highest court](https://ballotpedia.org/Court_of_last_resort "Court of last resort") in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois"). The court includes seven justices who are elected to 10-year terms in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election_of_judges "Partisan election of judges"). The court hears appeals from the lower courts and has limited original jurisdiction. It also serves as the administrative head of the state's court system.

### Political composition

This was the political composition of the supreme court heading into the 2020 election.

■[Anne M. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Anne_M._Burke "Anne M. Burke")_Appointed in 2006; elected in 2008_
■[Rita Garman](https://ballotpedia.org/Rita_Garman "Rita Garman")_Appointed in 2001; elected in 2002; retained in 2012_
■[Lloyd Karmeier](https://ballotpedia.org/Lloyd_Karmeier "Lloyd Karmeier")_Elected in 2004; retained in 2014_
■[Thomas Kilbride](https://ballotpedia.org/Thomas_Kilbride "Thomas Kilbride")_Elected in 2000; retained in 2010_
■[P. Scott Neville](https://ballotpedia.org/P._Scott_Neville "P. Scott Neville")_Appointed in 2018_
■[Mary Jane Theis](https://ballotpedia.org/Mary_Jane_Theis "Mary Jane Theis")_Appointed in 2010; elected in 2012_
■[Michael J. Burke](https://ballotpedia.org/Michael_J._Burke "Michael J. Burke")_Appointed in 2020_

## Selection

_See also: [Partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan\_elections "Partisan elections")_
The seven justices of the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") are chosen by popular vote in [partisan elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_elections "Partisan elections") and serve 10-year terms, after which they must compete in uncontested, nonpartisan [retention elections](https://ballotpedia.org/Retention_election "Retention election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6) Unlike most states, supreme court justices in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois") are elected to represent specific districts. The seven justices are divided among five districts (three allocated to [Cook County](https://ballotpedia.org/Cook_County,_Illinois_(Judicial) "Cook County, Illinois (Judicial)") and the others divided evenly among the other four districts) and are voted into office by the residents of their respective regions.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6) In the event of a midterm vacancy, the [Illinois Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court "Illinois Supreme Court") is responsible for appointing an interim justice. The interim justice serves until the next general election occurring at least 60 days after his or her appointment, at which point the justice must run in a [partisan election](https://ballotpedia.org/Partisan_election "Partisan election") to continue serving.[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6)

### Qualifications

To serve on the supreme court, a justice must be:

*   a U.S. citizen;
*   a district resident; and
*   licensed to practice law in [Illinois](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois "Illinois").[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/Illinois_Supreme_Court_elections,_2020?printable=yes#cite_note-gen-6)

### Selection of the chief justice

The [chief justice](https://ballotpedia.org/Chief_justice "Chief justice") of the supreme court is chosen by peer vote to serve a three-year term.
